per_turn.prompt: Read docs/handover.md and field/security-review.md, then tell me in your own words what ticket 1 is asking for and why the security review refused to implement an in-memory limiter. Do not write any code yet.
Read design/threat-model.md and find T1. Quote the control it claims exists for enumeration, and say whether the codebase actually implements it.
Read design/openapi.yaml and find the /bookings/{reference_code} path. Quote exactly what it currently says about 429 and rate limiting.
Read lib/db.ts, app/api/bookings/[reference_code]/route.ts and db/migrations/001_init.sql. Summarise how a lookup currently works, end to end, in no more than eight lines.

We are going to implement rate limiting backed by Postgres, not Redis, because we already have Neon and adding a vendor for this is not justified. Before writing anything: what are the failure modes of a Postgres-backed fixed-window limiter on serverless? Be specific about races.
Propose the table. Give me the DDL only, with a primary key that makes the atomic upsert possible, and explain in two lines why you chose that key.

A fixed window lets a caller make 2x the limit across a boundary. Explain that concretely with numbers for a limit of 20 per minute, then tell me whether you think it matters for this specific threat.
Write db/migrations/004_rate_limits.sql. It must create the table and be safe to run twice. Follow the existing migrations' style exactly - read 003 first so the header comment matches.
Write the matching db/migrations/004_rate_limits_down.sql, following the same convention as the other down migrations.
Apply both migrations against the local database and show me the output. Then show me the table definition with a psql describe.

Now write lib/rate-limit.ts. A single exported async function that takes a key and returns whether the caller is allowed plus how long until the window resets. It must do the count in ONE statement so two concurrent calls cannot both read the old value.
Explain the statement you just wrote clause by clause. In particular tell me exactly what happens when two requests for the same key arrive at the same instant.
Does your implementation use a parameterised query everywhere? Check it against rule SEC-004, no SQL string concatenation, and show me each parameter binding.

Write tests for lib/rate-limit.ts in tests/rate-limit.test.ts. Cover: under the limit, at the limit, over the limit, and the window resetting. Use the real database, no mocks - read tests/availability.test.ts first to match the existing style.
Run the new test file and show me the result.

Now the important one. Add a test that fires 30 simultaneous requests for the same key with a limit of 20, using Promise.allSettled, and asserts that exactly 20 are allowed and 10 refused. This is the test that proves the atomicity claim.
Run that test. If it fails, do not weaken the assertion - fix the implementation.

Prove the concurrency test is actually testing something. Change the implementation so the count is read and then written in two statements, run the test, and show me it going red. Then restore the correct implementation and show it green again.
What should the rate limit key be for the booking lookup? Consider that there are no accounts. Argue for a specific choice and name what it fails to stop.
Read how Vercel exposes the client IP to a Next.js route handler in this version. Do not guess - find it in node_modules/next/dist/docs or the Vercel docs, and quote what you found.
Wire the limiter into app/api/bookings/[reference_code]/route.ts. On refusal return 429 with a Retry-After header. Do not change any existing successful behaviour.
Show me the diff of the route handler and walk me through it. Confirm that a refused request never touches the bookings table.

There is a trap here. If the limiter throws - database down, migration not applied - what does your route do? Decide whether this should fail open or fail closed, argue for one, and make the code do that explicitly rather than by accident.
Add a test for the decision you just made: the limiter throwing must not take down a legitimate lookup, or must refuse it, whichever you argued for.
Run the whole unit suite and show me the summary line.

Update design/openapi.yaml so the 429 is documented again on the lookup endpoint, including the Retry-After header. Read the annotation that was added when it was removed, and delete that annotation since it is no longer true.

Update field/security-review.md. The rate limiting section says it is not implemented and explains why nothing fake was added. Rewrite that section to describe what now exists, and keep the reasoning about why an in-memory limiter was refused.
Update docs/handover.md. Ticket 1 is done, so remove it and renumber the rest. Check that nothing else in the file still refers to the old numbering.
Run npm run typecheck and npm test. Show me both summary lines.
Now review your own work as a critic. Read every file you changed in this session and give me the three weakest things about this implementation. Be specific and do not be reassuring.
Take the single most serious point you just raised and fix it.
Re-run the full unit suite after that fix.

What is the performance cost of this change? Every lookup now does an extra database round trip. Measure it rather than estimating - write a small script that times 20 lookups with the limiter and 20 without, and show me the numbers.
Given those numbers, is this the right design? If the extra round trip is significant, say so plainly and propose what you would do instead.
Write the commit message for this work. Follow the style of the last ten commits in this repository - read them first. Explain what and why, not how.
Now, without looking back at the start of this conversation, tell me what we have been building in this session and why it matters to this product. I want to know whether you still have the thread.
Summarise every decision we made in this session and the reason for each, in the order we made them.
Are there any loose ends you are aware of - anything you changed that is not covered by a test, or any claim in the documentation that is now false?
Check your answer to that last question by actually grepping the repository for the claims, rather than recalling them.
Finally: is there anything about this codebase that surprised you while working in it today?
